questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the allegorical function of a recurring figure in a support document.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-1042 asks why the onboarding wiki keeps returning to a figure in a yellow raincoat.

options.text: The raincoat stands for the old workflow, so one figure carries the argument about change.
The raincoat is weather gear mentioned since the office roof leaks by the north stairwell.
options.misconception: reads a recurring image as decorative detail

options.text: The raincoat begins a second story about a stranger who records what he sees in the building.
options.misconception: mistakes a repeated image for a subplot

options.text: The raincoat marks a date, so each appearance shows the wiki was written in a later year.
options.misconception: assumes recurrence marks a change in writing date

questions.explanation: An allegory gives a figure a sustained meaning so it can carry the argument, which is why the raincoat returns. Reading it as scenery, a subplot, or a dating marker severs it from that work.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a returning image at the close reframes its earlier meaning.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-1187 asks the docs team to explain why the migration guide ends by returning to the number thirty-three.

answer.exemplar: The closing paragraph reuses the count of thirty-three from the opening tutorial, so the number stops being a technical figure and becomes a marker of unfinished migration. Its return at the end tells the reader the process described is still incomplete, and the recurring image carries the guide's honest verdict on its own promise.

questions.explanation: A symbol at the ending gathers earlier meanings and delivers the final judgement. The repeated count implies the migration is incomplete, a verdict the opening only implied.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing image makes true.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a narrator whose smooth tone conceals a change in authorship.

stimulus.body: For eleven months the release notes were written by the platform team alone. In the twelfth month the writing passed to me, and I have kept the same cheerful register and the same insistence that every outage was instructive. I am told this continuity is a strength.

options.misconception: treats a consistent voice as proof of invention

questions.learningObjective: Identify a motif whose meaning changes between its first and last appearance.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the irony of a statement contradicted by the situation it describes.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-2601 asks the reviewer to explain why the handover note thanks the team for their patience.

answer.exemplar: The note thanks the team for patience during a handover that was itself the cause of the delay, so the gratitude is offered for a fault the writer knows the team performed. Because the situation supplies the contradiction that the words conceal, the sentence is ironic in situation rather than merely odd in phrasing, and the note's courtesy carries the opposite of its content.

questions.explanation: Irony of situation arises when what happens contradicts what is said about it, and patience that caused the delay inverts the thanks. Odd phrasing alone would not make the line ironic.

options.text: Each recurrence loosens the expectation, since repetition makes an image less noticeable over time.
options.misconception: claims repetition always reduces reader attention

options.text: Each recurrence tightens the expectation, since a motif seen often makes readers anticipate where it leads.
The recurrence has no effect, since the clock stands for time in every culture without help from the text.
options.misconception: treats a motif's force as purely conventional

options.text: The recurrence confirms a deadline, since the first line states that the project will end on a fixed day.
options.misconception: credits a stated fact for the trained expectation

questions.explanation: Motifs work by conditioning readers, so each return of the clock narrows what readers expect next. Diminished notice, purely conventional force, and a stated deadline each miss the training effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader begins anticipating.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a figure functions allegorically in a short procedural text.

stimulus.body: The safety notice tells the reader that the building has two doors, one for entering and one for leaving, and that each has been painted a different colour since the refit. The notice adds that painters working at height must never switch colours halfway through, because the next person cannot tell what the door does. The reviewer asked whether the doors can carry a symbolic meaning here.

questions.stem: Ticket ENG-3844 asks whether the two painted doors work as allegory in the safety notice.

options.text: They do, since every mention of a door in a notice about behaviour is automatically an allegory.
options.misconception: treats every repeated noun in a notice as allegory

options.text: They do, since the two colours stand for the two sides of the organisation's safety culture.
options.misconception: invents an organisational meaning the notice never supports

options.text: They do not, since the doors are explained practically and nothing in the notice asks for a second reading.
They do not, since allegory requires a whole narrative and a safety notice is too short to carry one.
options.misconception: confines allegory to long narrative forms

questions.explanation: Allegory needs a sustained second meaning beside the literal one, and this notice explains the doors without opening another layer. Invented symbolism and length requirements overreach.
questions.hint: Ask whether the notice supports a second layer of meaning.

options.misconception: attributes revision to a new character rather than an image

options.text: It cannot revise the claim, since an ending only confirms what the opening has established.

options.misconception: treats repetition alone as revision

answer.exemplar: The narrator describes the root cause as obvious and states that nobody could have seen it coming, then reports a recommendation made by a colleague whose own warning had been dismissed. options.text: It is ironic since the guide's stated purpose and its actual effect pull in opposite directions.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a narrator who reports the evidence but omits the judgement.

stimulus.body: Three engineers were in the room. The deploy pipeline was frozen for nineteen minutes and nobody spoke for the first four. options.misconception: treats an explicit gap as hiding rather than signalling

options.text: It should be judged as reliable, since a narrator who admits what they cannot know is trustworthy.
options.misconception: infers overall trustworthiness from admitted limits

options.text: The plain version is superior, since prose carries meaning that figures obscure for less technical readers.
options.misconception: claims prose always outruns figures in clarity

options.text: The plain version risks understating the scale, while the figures version risks one missing the point.
The figures version is superior, since readers who skip the numbers still receive the scale.
options.misconception: ignores that one may skip the numbers entirely

questions.explanation: Each voice solves the information problem differently, so one leans on readers' inference and the other on appetite for figures. Plain understatement and blanket superiority misjudge the options.
questions.hint: Ask where each version places the work of understanding.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the effect of shifting between registers in a single document.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6482 asks what a document gains by alternating between a formal register and a colloquial one.

options.text: It gains clarity, since one lost in formal prose can recover in the colloquial passages beside it.
options.misconception: confuses register contrast with remedial explanation

options.text: It gains nothing, since a document written in one register is always easier to trust than one that changes.
options.misconception: treats consistency as the only source of trust

options.text: It gains variety, since alternating registers keeps a long document from sounding monotonous to its readers.
options.misconception: reduces the effect to reader entertainment

options.text: It gains emphasis, since the formal passages set the standard against which the colloquial ones land harder.

questions.explanation: Register contrast creates emphasis, since the formal passages establish a measure the colloquial ones then break. Clarification and mere variety each misdescribe what the alternation produces.
questions.hint: Ask what the formal passages set up for the others.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a motif from a symbol by the difference in how each works.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6557 asks how the motif of harbour fog differs from the symbol of a harbour in the novel.

options.text: The fog repeats and gathers weight across appearances, while the harbour stands for one fixed idea throughout.
The fog stands for one fixed idea, while the harbour repeats and gathers weight across its appearances.
options.misconception: reverses the working of motif and symbol

options.text: Both work identically, since any repeated detail in a novel functions as a symbol with a fixed meaning.
options.misconception: collapses the two devices into one

options.text: Neither works, since only objects can carry symbolic weight in a novel and fog counts as weather.
options.misconception: restricts symbolism to man made objects

questions.explanation: A motif works by repetition that accumulates, while a symbol carries a settled charge in one image, so fog and harbour differ. Reversal and object-only rules each misstate the distinction.
questions.hint: Ask which one changes as it returns.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an allegorical reading is built from a character's repeated actions.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6681 asks the analyst to explain how the courier's actions construct an allegory in the training narrative.

answer.exemplar: The courier in the training narrative is shown refusing parcels, losing letters and arriving late, and in each case the failure is attributed to a rule rather than to carelessness. Those repeated actions build an allegorical figure for a system that treats every exception as a problem to be closed, which is precisely the claim the training is meant to make about how exception handling is really performed.

questions.explanation: Allegorical figures are built from what characters repeatedly do, and refusals caused by rules make the courier embody the system. A static type or a decorative character each miss it.
questions.hint: Ask what the courier does rather than what they are.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a final image completes an argument built by earlier symbols.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6745 asks how the closing image of a hand passing a key completes the argument about shared ownership.

options.text: It completes the argument by making the transfer explicit, so the story builds towards one handover.
options.misconception: reads the closing gesture as a simple confirmation

options.text: It completes the argument by showing the handover itself, so shared ownership ends as an act.
It completes nothing, since a key passed at the end of a story is practical detail, not symbolic.
options.misconception: dismisses the final image as literal detail

options.text: It completes the argument twice, since the handover both confirms shared ownership and contradicts it.
options.misconception: insists one image must carry opposing claims

questions.explanation: The closing image turns the argument on the moment of transfer, so a key handed over makes shared ownership an act. Literal detail and doubled meaning miss the single argument at work.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing gesture shows happening.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify irony of situation in a report about a helpful mistake.

stimulus.body: A team member deleted the wrong cache server during a routine clean up. The deletion released enough capacity that the following quarter's traffic surge, which had been predicted twice and ignored, was absorbed without incident. The report recommends the team buy a second cache server and continue clean ups as usual.

questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6898 asks why the report's clean and practical recommendation is ironic.

options.text: It is ironic since the report recommends more of the practice that caused the mistake in the first place.
options.misconception: confuses the irony with the recommendation's content

options.text: It is ironic since a report about capacity never recommends anything practical at the end of the document.
options.misconception: invents a rule that reports end differently

options.text: It is ironic since the good outcome was caused by an accident the report itself treats as ordinary.
It is not ironic, since an accident that happens to help is simply a lucky event with no further meaning.
options.misconception: denies that lucky accidents can be ironic

questions.explanation: Irony arises when the accidental and the deliberate are exchanged, and an unintended deletion produces the outcome the report treats as routine luck. Odd endings each miss the exchange.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the outcome nobody planned.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge a narrator's reliability across a whole retrospective account.
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-6924 asks how the retrospective account should finally be judged on reliability.

options.text: As unreliable everywhere, since a narrator who distorts once may distort any part of the account.
options.misconception: generalises any single flaw into total distrust

options.text: As reliable, since the account contains dates and figures that can be checked against other records.
options.misconception: treats checkable details as proof of a trustworthy whole

options.text: As reliable in method but not in conclusion, since only the ending of an account is ever in doubt.
options.misconception: confines doubt to the final pages of an account

options.text: As unreliable in a patterned way, since the distortions cluster around decisions the narrator personally made.

questions.explanation: Reliability is patterned, and distortions that cluster around the narrator's own decisions show interest rather than general confusion. Total distrust and doubt at the end misdescribe the account.
questions.hint: Ask where in the account the distortions gather.
